title: Cryptococcal meningitis: an antifungal induction network that does not connect, and a separate trial of when to start antiretroviral therapy
question: Among randomised trials in HIV-associated cryptococcal meningitis, what does each antifungal induction trial report for ten-week mortality, can those trials be joined into a network, and what does the separate trial of antiretroviral timing report?
_prose_rule: Prose may not restate a number the object holds structurally.
_staging_note: Each source is staged as a plain text extract, and a JSON wrapper beside it carries the same text with a hash of it. The registry points at the TEXT, because that is the file the gate hands a reviewer and the file every quoted sentence was read from. It previously pointed at the wrapper, which the gate deliberately withholds, so a checker following the registry would have been sent to a file no reviewer saw.
_sourcing_rule: Every MEASURED input carries the verbatim sentence it was read from. Where a source is behind a paywall, that is recorded on the source and on every block the restriction touches, and no figure is carried beyond what the accessible text states.
_estimand_rule: Three different estimands appear here and none is converted into another: two absolute risk differences with one-sided bounds, and one hazard ratio. Where a risk ratio is computed from counts so two trials can be read side by side, it is flagged as derived and the trial's own estimand is carried beside it.
completeness_statement: Every trial named is held with its counts and its own estimand. Nothing was cited and then dropped, so there is no removal block and no quarantine. Claims previously attached to this topic are carried under claims_corrected rather than silently deleted.

network.reference_treatment_absent_because: A reference treatment is the node every other node is expressed against, and naming one presupposes that every node can reach it. In a graph that falls into more than one piece there is no such node, so naming one would assert a comparison that does not exist. Each trial has its own reference arm, and those are marked on the nodes.
network.single_study_loop_note: The one closed loop in this graph is drawn entirely by the multi-arm trial. Every edge in it comes from one randomised population, so the loop carries no independent indirect evidence and supports no incoherence assessment. A loop count above zero must not be read here as evidence that could be checked against itself.
network.edges_are_the_trials_own_contrasts: The multi-arm trial contributes the two comparisons it framed, both against its own reference arm. The third pairwise comparison among its strategies is ALSO recoverable, because the source publishes an arm-level count and denominator for each of the three strategies, and it is recorded beside them as a within-trial contrast. An earlier version of this object declined it on the ground that the trial did not frame it. That ground was STRICTER THAN THE HANDBOOK and a reviewer was right to say so: chapter 23 states that where summary data are provided for each intervention group it does not matter how the groups were combined in the reported analyses, and that review authors do not need to analyse the data the same way the study authors did. What remains true is the unit-of-analysis constraint under 23.3.4: the three contrasts come from one randomised population and share arms, so none of them may be entered alongside another as though it were an independent study. That is not the same as saying they may never be combined at all, and an earlier version of this text said so wrongly; the section lists accounting for the correlation, and network meta-analysis, as routes that do permit it. The third is held as a contrast rather than as an independent edge.

third_within_trial_contrast.what_changed: This block used to carry the contrast's own point and interval beside the outcomes rather than among them, which duplicated a value in two places -- the defect this batch spends most of its rounds removing. It is now a full outcome with its own counts, its own recomputed estimate and its own edge in the graph, and this block only points at it.
third_within_trial_contrast.must_not_be_treated_as_independent: It shares participants with both other contrasts from the same trial. Entering any of the three alongside another as though it were a separate study is the unit-of-analysis error 23.3.4 names. Section 23.3.4 does list routes that would permit all three together -- accounting for the correlation, or a network meta-analysis -- so the constraint is on treating them as independent, not on holding them at all.

network.multi_arm_covariance_note: The multi-arm trial contributes two contrasts from one randomised population, sharing a control arm, so those contrasts are correlated and any synthesis using both would need the covariance between them. An earlier version of this object said that covariance COULD NOT BE CONSTRUCTED because the source publishes no variance for any arm. That was false, and false against this object's own arithmetic: it derives each contrast's standard error from the published counts, and on that same log risk-ratio approximation the shared-arm covariance is the reference arm's own contribution, one over its deaths minus one over its denominator, from the very same counts. A reviewer caught the contradiction. The covariance is available, and it is NOT the reason no synthesis is computed. The reason is that the graph does not connect.

multi_arm_covariance_value.derivation: one over the shared arm's deaths minus one over its denominator, on the log risk-ratio approximation this object already uses for the standard errors.
multi_arm_covariance_value.used_for: nothing here. It is recorded because the object previously claimed it was unobtainable, and a reader should be able to see that it is not.

network.why_no_network_estimate: The graph falls into separate pieces. Section 11.2.1 builds an indirect comparison through a treatment the two sets of trials have in common, and these trials share no node, so that construction has no input. Which regimen would have joined them is the part worth stating plainly: the one week of amphotericin B with flucytosine that the older trial found best, and that the World Health Organization adopted after it, is exactly the newer trial's control arm. The older trial holds it as one of five arms, and it is the arm whose numerator and denominator the accessible source does not publish. The break in this network is not a fact about the trials. It is a fact about what could be read.
network.status: disconnected; no network meta-analysis is possible and none is reported

handbook.decision: The timing trial is held as a separate two-arm comparison and is not placed in the antifungal network.
handbook.conformance: Every participant in it received the same antifungal induction; what was randomised is the day antiretroviral therapy started. Section 11.1.1 is where a network's nodes are defined: a network diagram consists of nodes representing the interventions and lines showing the available direct comparisons between pairs of them. This trial randomises none of the antifungal regimens, so it supplies no such line between them. An earlier version attached this to 11.2.2, which is TRANSITIVITY and makes no statement about what a node is; a reviewer was right that a correct decision was hanging from a claim its section does not make. Its outcome is analysed as time to death, which section 10.9 governs, and that is a different measure from the risk ratio used for induction, so the two are never combined.

network_excluded_trial.note: This trial is not excluded from the object. It is excluded from the antifungal graph, and it has its own outcomes.

bridge_that_would_have_connected_the_net.the_same_regimen_inside_acta: one of the two arms making up AMB1W_MIXED
bridge_that_would_have_connected_the_net.why_they_are_not_one_node: AMBITION-cm's control arm and one of ACTA's five arms are the same regimen, and AMBITION-cm's own discussion says its results are consistent with what ACTA reported for it. Treating ACTA's one-week node as that regimen would be wrong all the same, because ACTA's one-week node is half made of patients whose partner drug was fluconazole, and the trial reports the partner drug as a SUPERIORITY finding -- flucytosine better than fluconazole on ten-week mortality, with an interval excluding no effect -- while it reports the strategy comparisons as NON-INFERIORITY conclusions on two-week mortality. Those are different questions on different windows, so the source does not rank one against the other and neither does this object; what it does support is that the partner drug produced a demonstrated difference within the very node that would have to be treated as homogeneous. Splitting the node is what the network needs and what the accessible source cannot supply: the abstract reports the partner comparison only pooled across both amphotericin durations, and gives no numerator or denominator for any single arm.

methodological_authority.reference: Higgins JPT, Thomas J, Chandler J, Cumpston M, Li T, Page MJ, et al (editors). Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions version 6.5.1. Cochrane, 2025.
methodological_authority.version_checked_how: The publisher's own page for each chapter relied on was opened and its printed citation line read. The version and the dates below are what those lines say, not what an earlier build of this object assumed. The publisher's versions-and-changes page was read on the same day and is what settles which version is current: it lists 6.5.1 as the newest release line, with entries dated 2026 and 2025, above 6.5 dated 2024. Two of the publisher's own pages disagree with that and the disagreement is recorded rather than resolved: the Handbook landing page and the current-version index both still print version 6.5 updated August 2024. Where they conflict this object follows the version history and the per-chapter citation lines, because those are the more specific and the more recent statements, and the newest release listed under 6.5.1 revised a chapter this object does not cite.
methodological_authority.version_note: The Handbook is versioned as a whole AND dated per chapter, and the two do not move together: the table above gives each chapter the version and the last-updated date the publisher prints on it, and they are not the same as each other. An earlier version of this object named one version and one update month for the whole Handbook, and that pair matched neither the current version nor any date printed on the chapters actually relied on. Listing them chapter by chapter keeps the age of the authority behind each decision visible instead of averaged away; one of these chapters is a good deal older than the others.

sections_relied_on.used_for: What a node and a line in a network ARE: nodes are the interventions, lines the available direct comparisons between pairs of them. sections_relied_on.title: Risk of bias in studies with more than two groups
sections_relied_on.used_for: Its statement that where summary data are provided for each intervention group it does not matter how the groups were combined in the reported analyses, and that review authors need not analyse the data the way the study authors did. It is why the third within-trial contrast is recovered rather than declined for not having been framed. A review leg argued this sentence belongs to 23.3.2 instead. It does not, and the chapter was re-opened to check: the sentence sits between the 23.3.3 heading and the 23.3.4 heading, and 23.3.2 is titled Determining which intervention groups are relevant, not what that leg called it. The citation stands. A second leg then pressed the same point on THEMATIC grounds -- that a rule about extraction does not belong under risk of bias -- and that is a fair reading of the chapter's own organisation even though it does not move the sentence. So both are now cited, each for its own half: 23.3.2 for whether these groups are relevant to this review at all, 23.3.3 for the sentence that says the trialists' grouping does not bind us. A judge leg has now asserted the same relocation in four consecutive rounds, most recently calling this location claim factually incorrect, and in none of those rounds does its own list of files read contain a Handbook page. So the boundary is recorded here as quotation rather than as assertion. Section 23.3.3 opens: 'Bias may be introduced in a multiple-intervention study if the decisions regarding data analysis are made...'. It ends, immediately before the 23.3.4 heading: '...if the summary data are provided for each intervention group, it does not matter how the groups had been combined in reported analyses; review authors do not need to analyse the data in the same way as the study authors.' Anyone may open the chapter and check both.

sections_relied_on.title: Determining which intervention groups are relevant
sections_relied_on.used_for: Whether the third within-trial contrast is relevant to this review: the section asks which pair-wise comparisons of a multi-arm study would themselves meet the review's inclusion criteria. Both arms of that contrast are induction strategies inside this review's scope, so the comparison is relevant and is recovered.

sections_relied_on.title: How to include multiple groups from one study
sections_relied_on.used_for: The unit-of-analysis problem created by two contrasts sharing one reference arm, and the routes out of it, one of which is to account for the correlation. This is what governs the shared-control decision; an earlier version cited the indirect-comparison section, which both review families identified as the wrong one.

sections_relied_on.title: Indirect comparisons
sections_relied_on.used_for: The indirect path a common comparator makes available, and its absence when no node is shared.

sections_relied_on.title: Transitivity
sections_relied_on.used_for: The requirement that the sets of trials be similar in all important factors other than the comparison being made. It is about whether an indirect comparison is valid ONCE the nodes exist; it is not what decides what a node is.

sections_relied_on.title: Grouping variants of an intervention (defining nodes in the network diagram)
sections_relied_on.used_for: What actually governs whether a partner-mixed regimen and the flucytosine-partnered regimen may be ONE node: node definitions need careful consideration, maximising similarity within a node. An earlier version hung that decision on transitivity, which makes no statement about node grouping, and a reviewer was right about it.

sections_relied_on.title: What is incoherence?
sections_relied_on.used_for: Incoherence as the difference between a direct and an indirect estimate, which a graph with no closed loop cannot supply.

quotes: We randomly assigned HIV-infected adults with cryptococcal meningitis to receive an oral regimen (fluconazole [1200 mg per day] plus flucytosine [100 mg per kilogram of body weight per day] for 2 weeks), 1 week of amphotericin B (1 mg per kilogram per day), or 2 weeks of amphotericin B (1 mg per kilogram per day). Each patient assigned to receive amphotericin B was also randomly assigned to receive fluconazole or flucytosine as a partner drug.

Mortality in the oral-regimen, 1-week amphotericin B, and 2-week amphotericin B groups was 18.2% (41 of 225), 21.9% (49 of 224), and 21.4% (49 of 229), respectively, at 2 weeks and was 35.1% (79 of 225), 36.2% (81 of 224), and 39.7% (91 of 229), respectively, at 10 weeks.

The upper limit of the one-sided 97.5% confidence interval for the difference in 2-week mortality was 4.2 percentage points for the oral-regimen group versus the 2-week amphotericin B groups and 8.1 percentage points for the 1-week amphotericin B groups versus the 2-week amphotericin B groups, both of which were below the predefined 10-percentage-point noninferiority margin.

As a partner drug with amphotericin B, flucytosine was superior to fluconazole (71 deaths [31.1%] vs. 101 deaths [45.0%]; hazard ratio for death at 10 weeks, 0.62; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.45 to 0.84; P=0.002).
One week of amphotericin B plus flucytosine was associated with the lowest 10-week mortality (24.2%; 95% CI, 16.2 to 32.1).

handbook.decision: No network estimate and no indirect comparison is computed for antifungal induction.
handbook.conformance: Section 11.2.1 describes an indirect comparison as one made through a common comparator. These trials share no node, so that construction has no input. Whether a shared node COULD be forced into being by treating the one-week strategy as though it were the flucytosine-partnered regimen is a question about node GROUPING, and section 11.3.2.3 is what governs it: node definitions need careful consideration and should maximise similarity within a node. Half of that strategy received a different partner drug, and within that very node the trial demonstrated a difference: flucytosine better than fluconazole on ten-week mortality, with an interval excluding no effect. An earlier version called that the difference the trial found to matter MOST, which ranks it against strategy comparisons the trial reported as non-inferiority conclusions on a different window; the source states no such ranking and a reviewer was right to strike it. A demonstrated difference inside the node is enough on its own, so the two are not one node. An earlier version of this block argued that point from transitivity alone and a reviewer was right that transitivity does not settle what a node is. Once the nodes are fixed, section 11.2.2 refuses the forced merge for its own reason: it requires the sets of trials to be similar in all important factors other than the comparison being made, and half of that node received a different partner drug, which is the one difference the trial demonstrated INSIDE that node, on its own ten-week mortality comparison. No claim is made that it mattered more than anything else the trial tested; that would rank a superiority finding against non-inferiority conclusions on another window, which the source does not do. On loops, an earlier version of this object said the graph closed none. It does close one, and a reviewer was right to say so: the multi-arm trial supplies all three pairwise lines among its own strategies, which is the triangle section 11.1.1 describes a three-arm study as drawing. That loop still buys NO incoherence check, and the reason is not its absence but its provenance. Section 11.4.4.1 defines incoherence as the difference between the direct and the indirect estimate of the same comparison; here the indirect path runs through the third node of the SAME randomised population, so it is not independent evidence about the direct edge -- it is the same participants, arriving a different way. Comparing them would measure arithmetic, not disagreement between sources.

acta_oral_vs_2wk.not_poolable_reason: A single trial carries this comparison.
acta_oral_vs_2wk.shared_control_note: This contrast comes from a trial that randomised three strategies at once, so it shares whole arms with the trial's other contrasts, and sharing an arm means sharing those participants and their deaths. It shares the two-week strategy with the contrast of the one-week strategy against the two-week strategy. It shares the oral strategy with the contrast of the oral strategy against the one-week strategy. Each contrast is valid alone. Entering any of them alongside another as though it were a separate study would count the shared participants twice, which is why nothing here is added. Note this is NOT only a shared-REFERENCE-arm problem: one of these three contrasts never touches the trial's reference arm at all and still shares participants with both others.

shared_control_handbook.decision: The three contrasts from the multi-arm trial are reported separately and none is entered alongside another as though it were an independent study.
shared_control_handbook.conformance: These contrasts share whole ARMS, which is the general case; two of them also happen to share the trial's reference arm, and the third shares no reference arm with anything and is still correlated with both. An earlier version of this block said both contrasts leaned on the same reference arm, which stopped being true the moment a third contrast was recovered, and a reviewer caught it. Section 10.2 describes meta-analysis as combining studies that estimate the same quantity; these two estimate different quantities and share a denominator, so combining them would count those control participants twice and narrow an interval by borrowing precision that does not exist. The section that GOVERNS this is 23.3.4, on how to include multiple groups from one study: it names entering several comparisons so that the same comparator group appears more than once as the approach that must be avoided, calls it a unit-of-analysis error, and lists the ways out, one of which is to include the correlated comparisons and account for the correlation. An earlier version of this object cited 11.2.1 here. BOTH review families said that was wrong and both were right: 11.2.1 is Indirect comparisons, and two arms compared with a shared control inside ONE trial are DIRECT evidence, not indirect evidence. The correlation between them is real and is recorded with the network; it is simply not what that section is about.

NETWORK:disconnected-no-synthesis.decision: No network estimate and no indirect comparison is computed for antifungal induction.
NETWORK:disconnected-no-synthesis.conformance: Section 11.2.1 describes an indirect comparison as one made through a common comparator. These trials share no node, so that construction has no input. Whether a shared node COULD be forced into being by treating the one-week strategy as though it were the flucytosine-partnered regimen is a question about node GROUPING, and section 11.3.2.3 is what governs it: node definitions need careful consideration and should maximise similarity within a node. Half of that strategy received a different partner drug, and within that very node the trial demonstrated a difference: flucytosine better than fluconazole on ten-week mortality, with an interval excluding no effect. An earlier version called that the difference the trial found to matter MOST, which ranks it against strategy comparisons the trial reported as non-inferiority conclusions on a different window; the source states no such ranking and a reviewer was right to strike it. A demonstrated difference inside the node is enough on its own, so the two are not one node. An earlier version of this block argued that point from transitivity alone and a reviewer was right that transitivity does not settle what a node is. Once the nodes are fixed, section 11.2.2 refuses the forced merge for its own reason: it requires the sets of trials to be similar in all important factors other than the comparison being made, and half of that node received a different partner drug, which is the one difference the trial demonstrated INSIDE that node, on its own ten-week mortality comparison. No claim is made that it mattered more than anything else the trial tested; that would rank a superiority finding against non-inferiority conclusions on another window, which the source does not do. On loops, an earlier version of this object said the graph closed none. It does close one, and a reviewer was right to say so: the multi-arm trial supplies all three pairwise lines among its own strategies, which is the triangle section 11.1.1 describes a three-arm study as drawing. That loop still buys NO incoherence check, and the reason is not its absence but its provenance. Section 11.4.4.1 defines incoherence as the difference between the direct and the indirect estimate of the same comparison; here the indirect path runs through the third node of the SAME randomised population, so it is not independent evidence about the direct edge -- it is the same participants, arriving a different way. Comparing them would measure arithmetic, not disagreement between sources.

SHARED-CONTROL:contrasts-sharing-arms.decision: The three contrasts from the multi-arm trial are reported separately and none is entered alongside another as though it were an independent study.
SHARED-CONTROL:contrasts-sharing-arms.conformance: These contrasts share whole ARMS, which is the general case; two of them also happen to share the trial's reference arm, and the third shares no reference arm with anything and is still correlated with both. An earlier version of this block said both contrasts leaned on the same reference arm, which stopped being true the moment a third contrast was recovered, and a reviewer caught it. Section 10.2 describes meta-analysis as combining studies that estimate the same quantity; these two estimate different quantities and share a denominator, so combining them would count those control participants twice and narrow an interval by borrowing precision that does not exist. The section that GOVERNS this is 23.3.4, on how to include multiple groups from one study: it names entering several comparisons so that the same comparator group appears more than once as the approach that must be avoided, calls it a unit-of-analysis error, and lists the ways out, one of which is to include the correlated comparisons and account for the correlation. An earlier version of this object cited 11.2.1 here. BOTH review families said that was wrong and both were right: 11.2.1 is Indirect comparisons, and two arms compared with a shared control inside ONE trial are DIRECT evidence, not indirect evidence. The correlation between them is real and is recorded with the network; it is simply not what that section is about.
